title: Growth rate depends largely on water uptake (turgor) as well as metabolism

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Growth rate depends largely on water uptake (turgor) as well as metabolism

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A large part of growth, in animals and more conspicuously in plants, depends on turgor and osmotic conditions: the velocity of growth depends largely on the amount of water taken into the cells as well as on chemical metabolism.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: A large part of the phenomenon of growth, both in animals and still more conspicuously in plants, is associated with “turgor,” that is to say, is dependent on osmotic conditions; in other words, the velocity of growth depends in great measure (as we have already seen, p. 113) on the amount of water taken up into the living cells

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Osmotic factors in growth”. Scope: growing cells of plants and animals, especially plant elongation and early embryos

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-25: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.46

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The variables are measurable, but the stated breadth and vague effect size require interpretation. Existing experiments can test subsets, especially plant elongation, but no unified public dataset appears adequate for growing cells across plants and animals.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate cell-volume or organ elongation rates to water uptake, turgor, osmotic potential, and metabolic rate, then estimate the variance or causal response attributable to water status. The claim is supported where perturbations or time series show growth rate tracking water uptake after metabolic covariates are controlled.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Matched water-uptake, metabolism, and growth measurements are scattered.

The phrase 'in great measure' lacks a quantitative threshold.

Animal and plant mechanisms differ substantially.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.45
data adequacy: 0.3
data existence: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The Lockhart-style split between turgor and metabolism is a usable decision rule, but 'in great measure' still needs a chosen variance threshold. The relevant experiments exist for a few plant cells and early embryos and would have to be compiled from papers. They cover a small part of the stated scope, and water uptake is easily confounded with wall extensibility.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Partition growth velocity into a water-uptake or turgor term and a metabolic term, using osmotic or pressure clamps at fixed metabolism. A large drop in elongation when turgor is lowered at constant metabolism would support the claim; unchanged velocity under those clamps would refute the claim that water uptake carries a large share of the rate.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Turgor, water flux and metabolic rate are rarely published as a matched public table.

Volume increase from water can be a consequence of wall yielding rather than an independent driver.

Plant-cell experiments are much denser than measurements on animal embryos.
